q: Natural gas, an important source of organic compounds, consists mainly of:
x: Natural gas is mostly methane, CH₄, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane.

q: Coal tar, obtained by the destructive distillation of coal, is an important source of:
o: Aromatic compounds such as benzene, phenol and naphthalene
Natural gas consisting mainly of methane
x: Heating coal strongly in the absence of air gives coal gas, coal tar and coke. Coal tar is rich in aromatic compounds.

q: The very large number of organic compounds is mainly due to:
o: Carbon being a metal that forms many ions
Carbon's ability to form chains and rings and multiple bonds, together with isomerism
Carbon having the highest electronegativity of all elements
Organic compounds being made only by living things
x: Catenation, single, double and triple bonds, and the many isomers possible for one formula give millions of carbon compounds. Carbon is a non-metal and forms covalent bonds.

q: Most organic compounds dissolve more readily in:
o: Water than in any organic solvent
Molten salts than in organic solvents
Non-polar organic solvents such as benzene or ether than in water
x: Organic compounds are mostly covalent and non-polar or weakly polar, so 'like dissolves like': they dissolve in organic solvents. Some small polar ones, such as ethanol, also dissolve in water.

q: When most organic compounds are burnt completely in excess air, they give:
x: Organic compounds contain carbon and hydrogen, which burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O. CO forms only when oxygen is limited.

q: Solutions of most organic compounds, such as glucose or urea in water, do not conduct electricity because:
o: The compounds are covalent and do not ionise in solution
They contain too many oxygen atoms
They react with water to form metals
Their molecules are too heavy to move
x: Conduction in solution needs free ions. Most organic compounds are covalent non-electrolytes and stay as neutral molecules.

q: In methane, CH₄, the four C–H bonds point towards the corners of a:
o: Regular tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5°
Straight line, with a bond angle of 180°
x: A carbon atom with four single bonds (sp³) has its bonds directed to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, 109.5° apart.

q: Which compound is classed as organic even though it contains no hydrogen?
x: CCl₄ is a derivative of methane in which every H is replaced by Cl, so it is organic. CO, carbonates and carbides are studied as inorganic carbon compounds.

q: Benzene and its derivatives were called 'aromatic' compounds because many of the first ones known:
o: Were very good conductors of electricity
x: The name comes from the aroma of early compounds such as benzaldehyde. Today the term refers to the benzene-type ring, not the smell.

q: Which of the following is an alicyclic compound?
x: Cyclopentane has a ring of carbon atoms only and behaves like an alkane, so it is alicyclic. Benzene is aromatic, pyridine heterocyclic and hexane open-chain.

q: Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, is classified as:
x: Its four carbon atoms are joined one after another with no ring and no branch. Its isomer 2-methylpropane is the branched-chain form.

q: The heteroatom in the ring of furan, C₄H₄O, is:
x: Furan has a five-membered ring of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom. Pyrrole contains nitrogen and thiophene sulphur.

q: Aliphatic compounds are best described as:
o: Compounds that contain a benzene ring
Ring compounds that contain an atom other than carbon
Compounds made only of carbon atoms
Open-chain compounds, with straight or branched chains
x: Aliphatic means open-chain (acyclic). Alicyclic compounds are rings that resemble them in properties; benzene-ring compounds are aromatic.

q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, is classified as:
x: Propene has no ring, so it is open-chain, and its C=C double bond makes it unsaturated.

q: Which compound is correctly matched with its class?
x: Cyclobutane is a carbon-only ring that behaves like an alkane. Benzene is homocyclic aromatic, pyridine has a nitrogen in its ring, and propane is open-chain.

q: Phenol, C₆H₅OH, and cyclohexanol, C₆H₁₁OH, both contain a six-carbon ring. They differ in classification because:
o: Phenol is aromatic, while cyclohexanol is alicyclic
Phenol is alicyclic, while cyclohexanol is aromatic
Phenol is heterocyclic, while cyclohexanol is homocyclic
Phenol is open-chain, while cyclohexanol is closed-chain
x: Phenol's ring is a benzene ring, so it is aromatic. Cyclohexanol's ring is saturated, like cyclohexane, so it is alicyclic. Neither ring contains a heteroatom.

q: The functional group present in alcohols is:
x: Alcohols, such as ethanol CH₃CH₂OH, contain an –OH group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.

q: Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, belongs to the class of:
x: Replacing a hydrogen of an alkane by a halogen atom gives a haloalkane; the halogen atom is the functional group.

q: The functional group –CONH₂ is characteristic of:
x: –CONH₂ (a carbonyl joined to nitrogen) is the amide group, as in ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂. Amines have –NH₂ without the C=O.

q: Which functional group is present in both aldehydes and ketones?
x: Both contain C=O. In aldehydes it carries at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO); in ketones it lies between two carbon groups.

q: Which compound contains a carbonyl group but is NOT an aldehyde?
x: Butanone has its C=O between two carbon atoms, so it is a ketone. The other three have the –CHO group of aldehydes.

q: Which pair of compounds belong to the same class, having the same functional group?
x: Ethanol and propan-1-ol are both alcohols. The other pairs are alcohol and ether, aldehyde and ketone, and carboxylic acid and ester.

q: Propenoic acid (acrylic acid), CH₂=CHCOOH, contains which functional groups?
o: A carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group of an alcohol
A carbon–carbon double bond and a carboxyl group
A carbon–carbon double bond and an ester group
An aldehyde group and a hydroxyl group
x: CH₂=CH– is an alkene double bond and –COOH is the carboxyl group. Although –COOH contains C=O and –OH, together they form one carboxyl group, not a ketone and alcohol.

q: The two types of stereoisomerism are:
x: Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of atoms in space: geometric and optical. Chain, position and functional group isomerism are structural.

q: Maleic acid and fumaric acid both have the structure HOOCCH=CHCOOH but different properties. They are:
x: They differ only in the arrangement of the –COOH groups about the C=C bond: maleic acid is cis and fumaric acid is trans.

q: In trans-but-2-ene, the two methyl groups are:
o: On the same side of the C=C double bond
Both attached to the same carbon atom
At the two ends of a carbon ring
On opposite sides of the C=C double bond
x: Trans means 'across': the CH₃ groups lie on opposite sides. In cis-but-2-ene they lie on the same side.

q: Cis and trans isomers of an alkene do not change into each other at room temperature because:
o: Rotation about the C=C bond would require breaking the π bond
The two isomers have different molecular formulas
The C=C bond rotates freely and quickly
The isomers are always mirror images of each other
x: The π bond holds the two carbons in a fixed position; turning one end would break it, which needs much more energy than is available at room temperature.

q: Which compound is optically inactive?
x: In glycine the central carbon carries two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral. Each of the others has a carbon bonded to four different groups.

q: The rotation of plane-polarised light by an optically active compound is measured with a:
x: A polarimeter measures the angle and direction through which a solution rotates plane-polarised light.

q: Which statement about 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂, is correct?
o: It has cis and trans isomers, because it contains a C=C bond
It is optically active, because it contains a chiral carbon
It has no cis–trans isomers, because one doubly bonded carbon carries two identical CH₃ groups
It has cis and trans isomers, because it has three methyl groups
x: Geometric isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the C=C. Here one carbon carries two CH₃ groups, so swapping them gives the same molecule.
